title: How Much Does a Website Cost Per Month for a Small Business?
targetKeyword: how much does a website cost per month for a small business
excerpt: A small business website costs $30 to $700+ a month depending on who builds and runs it. Here is what each monthly cost covers and how to choose.

seo.metaTitle: How Much Does a Website Cost Per Month? (Small Business)
seo.metaDescription: A small business website costs $30 to $700+ a month. See what hosting, maintenance, updates and SEO really cost, with 3-year totals for each option.
keywords: how much does a website cost per month for a small business

body:
How much does a website cost per month for a small business? In most cases, between $30 and $700 a month. A DIY website builder costs $30 to $60 a month if you do the work yourself. A site built by an agency usually costs $50 to $300 a month to host and maintain after you have paid for the build. A done-for-you website subscription, where one company designs, builds and runs everything, typically costs $100 to $700 or more a month with nothing to pay upfront.

The right number depends less on the website itself and more on who does the work: you, a freelancer you call when something breaks, or a team that looks after it every month. This guide breaks down every monthly cost, shows real three-year totals, and helps you decide what your business should actually pay.

The quick answer: monthly website costs by option

OptionTypical monthly costUpfront costWhat you get
DIY website builder$30–$60$0Template, hosting and tools. You design, write and update it yourself.
One-off build + care plan$50–$300$2,000–$15,000Custom site, then hosting, backups and some updates. Bigger changes billed extra.
Website subscription$100–$700+Usually $0Design, build, hosting, security, updates and often SEO in one fee.

What you are actually paying for each month

Whichever route you choose, the same building blocks sit underneath every small business website. Knowing what each costs on its own helps you spot a fair price and avoid paying twice.

  • Domain name: about $10 to $20 a year for a .com or .co.uk, so roughly $1 to $2 a month. It should always be registered in your name.
  • Hosting: $5 to $50 a month. Cheap shared hosting is fine for a brochure site; booking systems and online stores need faster, more reliable hosting.
  • SSL certificate: often free with good hosting. Without it, browsers warn visitors your site is not secure.
  • Business email: about $6 to $7 per mailbox a month with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
  • Maintenance and security: $50 to $200 a month for backups, software updates, uptime and security monitoring. Skipping this is how small business sites get hacked or quietly break.
  • Content updates: agencies and freelancers usually charge $50 to $150 an hour for changes such as new prices, photos or pages.
  • SEO and Google Business Profile: ongoing local SEO is commonly a separate retainer of $300 to $1,500 a month.
  • Apps and add-ons: booking tools, forms, chat widgets and review apps each add $10 to $100 a month.

Add those up and a typical small business that buys everything separately spends $100 to $400 a month after launch, before any SEO, even though the website itself was already paid for.

Option 1: a DIY website builder ($30–$60 a month)

Builders such as Wix, Squarespace and Shopify are the cheapest way to get online. The monthly plan covers hosting, security and the editing tools, and many include a free domain for the first year.

The real cost is your time. Designing the site, writing the copy, setting up SEO and keeping it up to date can take 20 to 40 hours to start, and a few hours every month after. A DIY site makes sense if you have more time than budget, you need a simple site, and you are comfortable with design and writing. It struggles when you need custom booking, quote calculators or strong local search rankings in a competitive area.

Option 2: a one-off build plus a care plan ($50–$300 a month)

This is the traditional agency model. You pay $2,000 to $15,000 upfront for a custom website, then a smaller monthly fee for hosting and maintenance. The site is usually yours outright once it is paid for.

The catch is everything outside the care plan. Text changes, new pages, fixes after a plugin update and SEO are often billed separately. Many small businesses end up with a website that looked great at launch and is out of date two years later, because every change came with an invoice. Most one-off sites also need a redesign every three to five years, which means paying the upfront cost again.

Option 3: a website subscription ($100–$700+ a month)

With a website subscription, sometimes called website as a service, one company designs and builds your site and then runs it for a single monthly fee. Hosting, security, backups and content updates are included, and higher plans add booking systems, SEO and reporting. There is usually no upfront cost.

The trade-off is that you keep paying for as long as you use the service, and you need to check the contract carefully: how long is the minimum term, and what happens to the website if you cancel? We compare both models in detail in web design subscription vs one-time payment.

Real example: an 8-page website for a local plumber

Here is what the same website might cost over three years with each approach. Figures are typical, not quotes.

 DIY builderOne-off build + careSubscription
Upfront$0$6,000$0
Monthly$45 + $15 apps$100 care + ~$50 changes$199
Year 1 total$720$7,800$2,388
3-year total$2,160 + your time$11,400$7,164
Who keeps it updatedYouYou request and pay per changeIncluded

The DIY site is the cheapest in money but not in time. The one-off build costs the most in the first year. The subscription spreads the cost and includes the updates, but over five years or more a one-off site with light maintenance can work out cheaper, as long as you do not need many changes or a redesign.

Hidden monthly costs to watch for

  • Booking and marketplace fees: some booking apps charge per appointment or take a commission on new clients.
  • Payment and app fees: online stores pay transaction fees on top of the plan, plus monthly fees for each app.
  • Renewal price jumps: introductory hosting and builder prices often double on renewal.
  • Exit costs: some providers charge to transfer your site or keep the design when you leave. Ask before you sign.
  • Lost enquiries: a slow or outdated website costs you customers every month, which rarely shows up on an invoice.

How to decide what your business should pay

Start with what the website needs to do. If it is an online business card that rarely changes, a DIY builder or a simple one-off site is enough. If it needs to win enquiries every week, take bookings and rank in local search, budget for ongoing care, because a website like that is never really finished.

A useful rule of thumb: your website should pay for itself with one or two new customers a month. For a plumber, cleaner or clinic where a customer is worth hundreds of dollars, a $200 to $400 monthly plan that brings in even a few extra jobs is easy to justify. For a hobby business, it is not.

Ask any provider these questions: What exactly is included each month? How many changes can I request? Is there a minimum contract? Who owns the domain, content and design? What happens if I cancel?

What about the UK?

UK prices follow the same pattern: roughly £25 to £50 a month for a DIY builder, £2,000 to £10,000 upfront for an agency build, and £75 to £500 a month for a pay monthly website. See our guide prices for pay monthly websites for UK small businesses.

Frequently asked questions

What is a reasonable monthly cost for a small business website?

For a site you run yourself, $30 to $60. For a professionally built and maintained site, $100 to $400 is typical, and $400 to $700 or more when it includes SEO, booking systems or custom software.

How much is website maintenance per month?

Usually $50 to $200 a month for hosting, backups, security and small updates. Content changes beyond that are often billed hourly.

Is it cheaper to build a website once or pay monthly?

Paying once is often cheaper over five years or more if you rarely change the site. Paying monthly is cheaper in the first few years and includes updates and support, which matters if your website needs to keep winning customers.

title: Web Design Subscription vs One-Time Payment: Which Is Better?
targetKeyword: web design subscription vs one time payment
excerpt: Should you pay monthly for a website or buy it outright? An honest comparison of costs over 1, 3 and 5 years, ownership, and which suits your business.

seo.metaTitle: Web Design Subscription vs One-Time Payment (Honest Guide)
seo.metaDescription: Web design subscription vs one-time payment: costs over 1, 3 and 5 years, who owns the site, pros and cons, and the questions to ask before you sign.
keywords: web design subscription vs one time payment
pay monthly website vs one off
is a website subscription worth it

body:
Choosing between a web design subscription vs a one-time payment comes down to three things: how much cash you want to spend upfront, how often your website needs to change, and how much you care about owning everything outright. Neither option is always better. A one-time payment usually wins on long-term cost if your site rarely changes. A subscription usually wins when your website needs regular updates, SEO and support to keep bringing in customers.

We sell monthly plans, so we will be upfront about where a one-off build is the smarter choice. Here is an honest comparison.

How each model works

One-time payment

You pay an agency or freelancer a fixed price, typically $2,000 to $15,000 for a small business site, and they design and build it. Once it is paid for, the website is usually yours. Hosting, maintenance and future changes are separate: you either manage them yourself or pay for a care plan and hourly updates.

Web design subscription

You pay a monthly fee, often $100 to $700, and the provider designs, builds, hosts and maintains the site for as long as you subscribe. Updates, security and support are included, and many plans add SEO, booking systems or reporting. There is usually little or no upfront cost. This model is also called website as a service or a pay monthly website.

Cost over 1, 3 and 5 years

Here is a realistic comparison for a small service business website. The one-off example assumes an $8,000 build and $100 a month for hosting and maintenance, with updates billed on top.

 One-off ($8,000 + $100/mo)Subscription $199/moSubscription $399/mo
Year 1$9,200$2,388$4,788
Year 3$11,600$7,164$14,364
Year 5$14,000$11,940$23,940
Extra changesBilled per change10 a month includedUnlimited
SEO, booking, reportingExtraSEO setup onlyIncluded

Two things stand out. First, the subscription is far cheaper in the early years, which matters if cash flow is tight. Second, a higher-tier subscription can cost more than a one-off build over five years, but it also includes work, such as ongoing SEO and booking systems, that would cost thousands extra with a one-off site. Compare like for like: the question is not just the price of the website, but the price of everything you need it to do.

Also remember that most one-off websites are redesigned every three to five years. If you count a second build in year four, the one-time payment often stops being the cheaper option.

Pros and cons of a one-time payment

  • Pro: you usually own the website outright once it is paid for.
  • Pro: lower total cost over many years if the site rarely changes.
  • Pro: you can move hosting or developers whenever you like.
  • Con: a large upfront cost, usually thousands of dollars.
  • Con: changes, fixes and SEO cost extra, so sites tend to go out of date.
  • Con: you are responsible for security, updates and backups, or for paying someone to handle them.

Pros and cons of a web design subscription

  • Pro: little or nothing upfront, with a predictable monthly cost.
  • Pro: updates, hosting, security and support are included, so the site keeps improving.
  • Pro: one team is responsible for results, not just for launch day.
  • Con: you pay for as long as you use the service.
  • Con: ownership terms vary: some providers keep the design if you leave.
  • Con: long minimum contracts with some providers make it hard to switch.

The ownership question

This is the most important thing to check with any subscription. At minimum, your domain name should be registered in your name, and your logo, content and customer data should always belong to you. What varies is the website design and code. Some providers let you buy the site out or transfer it when you leave; others keep it, and you start again elsewhere.

Neither is wrong, but you should know before you sign. At Velaris, your domain is registered in your name, your content and data are yours, and what happens to the website if you cancel is written into your proposal before we start. Plans are month-to-month with 30 days' notice.

Which should you choose?

Choose a one-time payment if

  • You have the budget upfront and want to own everything outright.
  • Your website is mostly informational and rarely changes.
  • You have someone in-house, or a developer you trust, to maintain it.

Choose a subscription if

  • You would rather keep cash for marketing, staff or equipment.
  • Your website needs to win enquiries every week and change as your business grows.
  • You want booking, SEO and updates handled without managing several suppliers.
  • You want a professional site now rather than saving for one.

Questions to ask before you sign

  1. What is included each month, and how many changes can I request?
  2. Is there a setup fee or a minimum contract term?
  3. Who owns the domain, content, design and code?
  4. What happens to the website if I cancel? Can I buy it out or transfer it?
  5. How quickly do you make changes, and how do I request them?
  6. What happens to the price after the first year?

The bottom line

If you want the lowest cost over many years and your site rarely changes, pay once. If you want no upfront cost and a website that is kept fast, secure and improving every month, a subscription is usually the better fit, as long as the ownership and cancellation terms are clear.
